(Fāʾidah)

As for placing al-Ghafūr before al-Raḥīm, it is more natural, because forgiveness (maghfirah) is safety and mercy (raḥmah) is gain, and safety is sought before gain. In the hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ:

"I send you on a mission in which Allah will keep you safe and grant you gain, and I desire for you a generous portion of wealth."

(Ṣaḥīḥ)

This is a wonderful ordering: it begins with safety before gain, and gain before acquisition.

As for His saying, ﴿And He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware﴾ — no, rather ﴿And He is the Merciful, the Forgiving﴾ — here mercy precedes forgiveness, either because of its excellence and perfection, or by nature, since it is connected to the mention of the kinds of creation, including the responsible (mukallafūn) and others among the animals: mercy encompasses them all, while forgiveness is specific to them, and the general precedes the specific by nature.

(Faṣl)

As for placing al-Raḥīm before al-Ghafūr in one place only, namely at the beginning of Sabaʾ, there is in it a meaning other than what al-Suhaylī mentioned, which becomes evident to whoever reflects on the context of His sublime attributes and beautiful names at the beginning of the surah up to His saying, ﴿And He is the Merciful, the Forgiving﴾. He, glory be to Him, began the surah with His praise, which is the most comprehensive of knowledge and the broadest of sciences, and which includes all the attributes of His perfection and the descriptions of His majesty, and entails them, just as it includes His wisdom in all His acts and commands. He is praised in every state and for everything He created and legislated. Then He followed this praise with His wide and extensive dominion, saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. Then He followed it with the statement that this praise is established for Him in the Hereafter, never ceasing forever, for it is praise He deserves by His essence and the perfection of His attributes, and what one deserves by his essence endures as long as He endures and never passes away. He joined dominion and praise, according to His customary manner in His speech, for the connection of each with the other carries a perfection beyond the perfection of each one alone: He has perfection from His dominion, perfection from His praise, and perfection from the combination of the two. Dominion without praise implies deficiency, and praise without dominion implies incapacity, while praise together with dominion is the utmost perfection. Similar to this are might and mercy, pardon and power, self-sufficiency and generosity. He placed dominion between the two phrases, enclosing it with praise before it and praise after it. Then He followed this praise and dominion with the names al-Ḥakīm (the All-Wise) and al-Khabīr (the All-Aware), which indicate the perfection of will, that it is never directed toward an object except for a far-reaching wisdom, and the perfection of knowledge, that just as it relates to the outward aspects of things known, it also relates to their inward aspects, which are only perceived through His awareness. Thus the relation of wisdom to will is like the relation of awareness to knowledge: the object willed is outward and the wisdom is inward; knowledge is outward and awareness is inward. The perfection of will is that it occurs in accordance with wisdom, and the perfection of knowledge is that it unveils inner awareness. So awareness is the inner dimension and perfection of knowledge, and wisdom is the inner dimension and perfection of will.

Thus the verse establishes His praise, His dominion, His wisdom and His knowledge in the most perfect manner.

Then He mentioned the details of His knowledge of what appears and what is hidden in the upper and lower worlds, saying: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends into it﴾. Then He concluded the verse with two attributes that entail the utmost kindness toward His creation, namely mercy and forgiveness: He brings them benefit and good in the most complete way through His mercy, pardons their slips, grants them their sins and does not hold them accountable for them through His forgiveness. So He said: ﴿And He is the Merciful, the Forgiving﴾.

This verse thus includes the breadth of His knowledge, mercy, wisdom and forgiveness. He, glory be to Him, joins breadth of knowledge with mercy just as He joins knowledge with forbearance. Of the first is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You encompass everything in mercy and knowledge﴾. Of the second is: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing﴾.

Nothing is joined to something more beautifully than forbearance to knowledge, and mercy to knowledge.

The bearers of the Throne are four: two say, "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You; to You belongs all praise for Your forbearance after Your knowledge," and two say, "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You; to You belongs all praise for Your pardon after Your power." Thus the joining of pardon with power is like the joining of forbearance and mercy with knowledge, because pardon is only fitting when one has power, and likewise forbearance and mercy are only fitting with knowledge. He placed al-Raḥīm (the Merciful) first in this place because of the precedence of the attribute of knowledge; so mentioning al-Raḥīm after it fits, to be paired with it, corresponding to His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You encompass everything in mercy and knowledge﴾.

Then He concluded the verse with mention of the attribute of forgiveness, because it includes the averting of evil, whereas what precedes it includes the bringing of good.

Since averting evil takes precedence over bringing good, He placed al-Ghafūr before al-Raḥīm wherever they occur. But since in this place there is a conflict that requires placing His name al-Raḥīm first on account of what precedes it, He placed it before al-Ghafūr.

(Fāʾidah: on the singular and plural of "heaven")

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And not an atom's weight in the earth or in the heaven escapes your Lord﴾ [Yūnus: 61].

This differs from His saying in Sabaʾ: ﴿The Knower of the unseen, from whom not an atom's weight escapes in the heavens or in the earth﴾. For before the latter He mentioned the breadth of His dominion and its scope, which is all the heavens and the earth. Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 34, verse 13:

Allah, glory be to Him, described the grateful (al-shakirin) as being few among His servants, so He said, ﴿And few of My servants are grateful.﴾

Imam Ahmad narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard a man say, "O Allah, make me among the few (al-aqallin)." He said, "What is this?"

The man said, "O Commander of the Faithful, Allah said, ﴿And none believed with him except a few.﴾"

And Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And few of My servants are grateful.﴾

And He said, ﴿Except those who believed and did righteous deeds, and few are they.﴾

So Umar said, "You are right." And Allah, glory be to Him, praised the first messenger He sent to the people of the earth with gratitude, so He said, ﴿The offspring of those We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾

(Lata'if, a subtle point)

Mush'ir said: When it was said to the family of Dawud, ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude,﴾ there did not pass over the people an hour except that among them was one praying.

Awn ibn Abd Allah said: Some jurists said, "I have looked into my affairs and have not seen any good except that it is accompanied by evil, except well-being (al-mu'afah) and gratitude. For many a grateful person is in his trial, and many a person in well-being is not grateful. So when you ask Allah, ask Him for both of them together."

Ahmad said: Yasar narrated to us, Hafs narrated to us, Thabit narrated to us: Dawud, peace be upon him, had divided the hours of the night and the day among his family, so there was not an hour of night or day but that someone from the family of Dawud was standing in prayer during it. He said: So Allah, blessed and exalted, included them in this verse: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude, and few of My servants are grateful.﴾

Ahmad said: Jabir ibn Zayd narrated to us from al-Mughirah ibn Uyaynah, who said: Dawud said, "O Lord, has any of Your creation spent the night remembering You longer than I have?" Allah revealed to him, "Yes, the frog." And Allah sent down to him, ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude, and few of My servants are grateful.﴾

He said, "O Lord, how can I manage to thank You, when You are the One who bestows favors upon me, then You provide me with gratitude for the favor, then You increase me in favor after favor? The favors are from You and the gratitude is from You. So how can I manage to thank You?" He said, "Now you have known Me, O Dawud."

Ahmad said: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, al-Rabi' ibn Subayh narrated to us from al-Hasan, who said: The Prophet of Allah Dawud said:

"My God, if every hair of mine had two tongues glorifying You night and day and throughout time, I would not have fulfilled the right of a single favor."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned from Abu Imran al-Jawni, from Abu al-Khald, who said: Musa said, "O Lord, how can I thank You, when the smallest favor You have placed with me from Your favors is not repaid by all my deeds?" So revelation came to him: "O Musa, now you have thanked Me."

Bakr ibn Abd Allah said: No servant has ever said "All praise is due to Allah" except that a favor became due upon him by his saying "All praise is due to Allah." So the reward for that favor is that he says "All praise is due to Allah," and then another favor comes, and the favors of Allah do not run out.

(Fa'idah, a benefit)

The station of gratitude (maqam al-shukr) comprises all the stations of faith, and for this reason it is the highest and loftiest of them. It is above contentment (al-rida), and it includes patience (al-sabr) without the reverse being true. It includes reliance (al-tawakkul), turning in repentance (al-inabah), love (al-hubb), humility (al-ikhbat), submissiveness (al-khushu') and hope (al-raja'). All the stations are contained within it. Its possessor does not deserve his name absolutely except by combining the stations in himself. For this reason faith has been described as two halves: half patience and half gratitude, and patience is included within gratitude, so all of faith returns to gratitude. The grateful are the fewest of the servants, as the Exalted said, ﴿And few of My servants are grateful.﴾ [Saba': 13]

(Lata'if, a subtle point)

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah was asked about preferring the wealthy grateful person over the poor patient person, or the reverse. He answered in a way that heals hearts, saying: "The more excellent of the two is the one more God-fearing (atqahuma) before Allah, the Exalted. If they are equal in piety, they are equal in rank."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 34, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And he had no authority over them, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it.﴾

So He did not give His enemy any authority over His believing servants, for they are in His protection, His guardianship, His safekeeping, and under His care. If His enemy ambushes one of them, as a thief ambushes a heedless man, this is unavoidable, because the servant has been afflicted with heedlessness, desire, and anger, and the enemy enters upon the servant through these three doors, however much the servant guards himself. So there must be heedlessness for him, there must be desire for him, and there must be anger for him.

Adam, father of mankind (ﷺ), was among the most forbearing of creation, the soundest in intellect, and the steadiest. Yet the enemy of Allah did not cease to work on him until he brought him down into it. So what is to be thought of a speck of forbearance and an intellect such as ours, compared with the intellect of his father, like a spittle in the sea? But the enemy of Allah does not reach the believer except by stealth, catching him unawares and in heedlessness. He brings him down and thinks that he will not stand before his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, after it, and that this fall has destroyed and ruined him. Yet the grace of Allah, His mercy, His pardon and His forgiveness lie beyond all of that.

When Allah wills good for His servant, He opens for him the doors of repentance, remorse, humility, abasement, dependence, seeking help from Him, sincere turning to Him, constant supplication and entreaty, and drawing near to Him through as many good deeds as possible, so that this sin becomes, through His mercy, something else. Then the enemy of Allah says: "Would that I had left him and not brought him down."

This is the meaning of the saying of some of the Salaf: "A servant may commit a sin by which he enters Paradise, and perform a good deed by which he enters the Fire."

They said: "How?"

He said: "He commits a sin, and it does not cease to be before his eyes, so that he is fearful, trembling, weeping, regretful, shy before his Lord, may He be exalted, head bowed before Him, his heart broken before Him. That sin is more beneficial to him than many acts of obedience, because of what follows from it of these matters by which the servant attains happiness and success, until that sin becomes the cause of his entering Paradise."

"And he performs a good deed, and does not cease to act as if he were bestowing favour upon his Lord by it, taking pride in it, admiring himself, being impressed by it, exalting himself through it, saying: 'I did this and I did that.' So it bequeaths to him conceit, pride, boastfulness and self-exaltation, which become the cause of his ruin."

When Allah, may He be exalted, wills good for this wretched one, He tests him with something by which He breaks him, humbles his neck by it, and diminishes his self in his own eyes. But if He wills otherwise for him, He leaves him to his self-admiration and pride. This is the abandonment (khidhlan) that necessitates his destruction.

For the knowers ('arifun) are all agreed that tawfiq (divine enabling) is that Allah, may He be exalted, does not leave you to yourself, and khidhlan (abandonment) is that Allah, may He be exalted, leaves you to yourself.

So whoever Allah wills good for, He opens for him the door of humility and brokenness, constant turning to Allah, the mhhhh... need for Him, seeing the defects of his own self, its ignorance and its transgression, and witnessing the bounty, goodness, mercy, generosity, kindness, self-sufficiency and praiseworthiness of his Lord.

So the knower journeys to Allah, may He be exalted, between these two wings, and he cannot travel except with both. Whenever he loses one of them, he is like a bird that has lost one of its wings.

The Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyya) said: "The knower travels to Allah between witnessing the favour (minnah) and observing the defect of the self and of works."

(Section)

When the enemy of Allah knew that Allah, may He be exalted, would not give him power over the people of tawhid and sincerity, he said: ﴿So by Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them.﴾ [Sad: 82-83]

So the enemy of Allah knew that whoever holds fast to Allah, the Mighty, sincerely devotes himself to Him, and relies upon Him, he cannot make him stray or mislead him. Rather, he has authority only over those who take him as a guardian and associate others with Allah. These are his subjects, and he is their guardian, their ruler, and their leader.

If it is said: "You have affirmed his authority over his allies in this place. So how does he negate it in His saying:

﴿And Iblis had certainly confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except a party of believers. And he had no authority over them, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it.﴾ [Saba: 20-21]"

It is answered: If the pronoun in His saying ﴿And he had no authority over them﴾ [Saba: 21] refers to the believers, then the objection falls away, and the exception is disjunctive (munqati'): i.e., "but We tested them through Iblis, so that We might know who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it." If it refers to what the pronoun referred to in His saying ﴿And Iblis had certainly confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him﴾ [Saba: 20], it is the apparent reading, so that the disjunctive exception is valid, occurring after a negation, and the meaning is: "We did not give him power over them except that We might know who believes in the Hereafter."

Ibn Qutayba said: "When Iblis asked Allah for respite, he said: 'I will surely mislead them, I will surely lead them astray, I will surely command them to such-and-such, and I will surely take from Your servants a appointed portion.' At the time of this statement he was not certain that what he had decreed about them would be accomplished; he spoke only by conjecture. When they followed him and obeyed him, what he had assumed of them came true. So Allah, may He be exalted, said: 'And We did not give him power over them except that We might know those who believe from those who doubt,' meaning: We know them existing and manifest, so the word is realized and the recompense occurs."

On this basis, the authority here is over those who do not believe in the Hereafter and doubt it, namely those who took him as a guardian and associated others with Him. Thus the authority is affirmed, not negated, and this verse agrees with the rest of the verses.

If it is said: "Then what do you make of the verse in Surat Ibrahim, where he says to the people of the Fire:

﴿And I had no authority over you, except that I called you, and you responded to me.﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]"

And this, although it is his statement, Allah, may He be exalted, reported it as confirming it for him, not denying it, which indicates that it is so.

It is answered: This is a good objection. Its answer: the authority negated in this place is proof and evidence, i.e., "I had no proof or evidence against you by which I could argue against you," as Ibn 'Abbas said: "I had no proof by which I could argue against you," meaning: I showed you no proof, except that I called you and you responded to me, and accepted my statement, and followed me without proof or evidence.

As for the authority that he affirmed in His saying: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as a guardian﴾ [al-Nahl: 100], it is his domination over them through misleading and leading astray, and his establishment over them, such that he drives them toward disbelief and polytheism and urges them to it, and does not leave them to abandon him, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Have you not seen that We sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ [Maryam: 83]

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They incite them with incitement." In another narration: "They urge them with urging." In another wording: "They spur them on with spurring." In another: "They drive them to sins with driving." In another: "They kindle them," i.e., they stir them as water is stirred by a fire beneath it. Al-Akhfash said: "They heat them up."

Consider how this verse closes off the main avenues through which the polytheists entered into shirk, sealing the door against them in the most complete and firm way. The worshipper only attaches himself to the one worshipped because of the benefit he hopes to obtain from it; were he not hoping for any benefit from it, his heart would never attach itself to it at all. Given this, the one worshipped must be one of the following: either an owner of the means by which his worshipper benefits, or a partner of its owner, or a helper, minister or assistant to him, or a dignitary of standing and rank who intercedes with him. When these four matters are completely negated, the causes of shirk are eliminated and its roots are cut off.

So God, glory be to Him, negated from their gods that they possess even an atom's weight in the heavens and the earth.

The polytheist may say: "They are partners of the true Owner." So He negated their partnership with Him.

The polytheist may say: "They may be helpers, ministers or assistants." So He said: ﴿And He has no supporter among them﴾.

Nothing remained but intercession, so He negated it for their gods, and informed that no one intercedes with Him except by His permission. If He does not permit the intercessor, the intercessor does not advance to intercede before Him, as happens with created beings. For the one interceded with among creatures needs the intercessor and his assistance, so he accepts his intercession even if he has not granted him permission for it. As for everything other than Him, it is needy of Him in its very essence, while He is self-sufficient in His essence beyond everything else. How, then, could anyone intercede with Him without His permission?

(Section)

God, exalted is He, has cut off all the causes on which the polytheists relied, entirely, with a severing that whoever reflects upon it and understands it will know: whoever takes, besides God, a protector or an intercessor is like the spider that takes a house, and indeed the weakest of houses is the spider's house. Thus God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claim besides God. They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth, nor do they have any share in them, nor is there among them any supporter for Him. And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He has permitted﴾ [Saba': 22–23].

The polytheist only takes his object of worship because he believes that benefit will come to him from it, and benefit comes only from one who possesses one of these four qualities: either he is an owner of what his worshippers seek from him; if he is not an owner, he is a partner of the owner; if he is not a partner, he is a helper and supporter; and if he is neither helper nor supporter, he is an intercessor with Him.

Thus God, glory be to Him, negated the four ranks in a sequenced negation, descending from the highest to what is below it: He negated ownership, partnership, support, and the intercession that the polytheist imagines, and He affirmed an intercession in which no polytheist has any share, namely intercession by His permission.

This verse is therefore sufficient as a light, a proof, a means of salvation, and a purification of tawhid, and a severing of the roots of shirk and its consequences for whoever understands it. The Qur'an is full of its like and its parallels. But most people do not perceive that the reality in question falls under it and is contained in it, and they suppose it refers to a type of people and a folk who passed away before, leaving no heirs. And this is what stands between the heart and understanding the Qur'an.

The polytheist only takes his object of worship because he believes that benefit will come to him from it, and benefit comes only from one who possesses one of these four qualities: either he is an owner of what his worshippers seek from him; if he is not an owner, he is a partner of the owner; if he is not a partner, he is a helper and supporter; and if he is neither helper nor supporter, he is an intercessor with Him.

Thus God, glory be to Him, negated the four ranks in a sequenced negation, descending from the highest to what is below it: He negated ownership, partnership, support, and the intercession that the polytheist imagines, and He affirmed an intercession in which no polytheist has any share, namely intercession by His permission.

This verse is therefore sufficient as a light, a proof, a means of salvation, and a purification of tawhid, and a severing of the roots of shirk and its consequences for whoever understands it. The Qur'an is full of its like and its parallels. But most people do not perceive that the reality in question falls under it and is contained in it, and they suppose it refers to a type of people and a folk who passed away before, leaving no heirs. And this is what stands between the heart and understanding the Qur'an.

(A subtle point)

Consider His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾.

For the path of truth rises upward, carrying its companion high towards the Most High, the Great, while the path of error descends downward, dropping its traveller into the lowest of the low.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 34, verse 37:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not your wealth nor your children that bring you near to Us in position, except for those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾

Here, "those who believe" (man amana) is not included within "wealth and children," but it is a statement constructed according to its meaning (min al-kalam al-mahmul ʿala al-maʿna). For He, may He be exalted, informed that the wealth and children of people do not bring them near to Him, and this implies that their owners are not among those brought near to Him. So He made an exception from them: "except those who believe and do righteous deeds."

That is, there is no one near to Him except those who believe and do righteous deeds, whether or not he possesses wealth and children. The disjunctive (al-infisal) reading is clearer here, for He negated people's nearness to Him through their wealth and children, and affirmed their nearness to Him through their faith and righteous deeds. Thus the estimation of "lakin" (but) here is clearer than the estimation of continuity (al-ittisal) in this exception.

When you reflect upon Arabic speech, you will find much of it coming in accordance with meaning because the meaning is clear; for if it came in accordance with the strict form of the wording while the meaning was clear, it would be a defect (ʿayy) in expression.

By this principle, many of your difficulties will dissolve, and you will not need to force the far-fetched estimations (al-taqdirat) which the speaker himself turned away from because of the burden of mentioning them. The over-burdened ones estimated for his speech what he fled from, and obligated him with what he had averted from.

This is common in the estimations of the grammarians (al-nuhat), which never occur to the speaker at all, and do not appear in the constructions of eloquent speakers; and if they heard them, they would find them objectionable.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 34, verse 46:

Since a person who seeks knowledge of the truth and the correct position has two states:

The first: that he is reflecting alone with himself.

The second: that he is debating with others.

[God] commanded them with one single quality, which is that they stand up for God in pairs, two by two, so that they debate and question one another, and individually, each one standing alone with himself, so that he reflects on the matter of this caller and what he calls to, and summons the proofs of truthfulness and falsehood, and presents what he has brought to them, so that the reality of the situation becomes clear to him.

This is the noble argumentation (hijaj), the clear fairness (insaf), and the complete sincere counsel (nasihah).

(Section)

The one who reflects (al-nazir) has two states: one in which he is praised and one in which he is blamed.

The debater (al-munazir) likewise has two states. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: I admonish you with one thing: that you stand up for God in pairs and individually, then reflect: there is no madness in your companion.﴾

So by their standing in pairs He pointed to debate (al-munazarah), and individually to reflection and contemplation (al-nazar wa-al-tafakkur). Each of these is divided into praiseworthy and blameworthy.

Praiseworthy reflection is reflection on the correct path, by which one reaches knowledge of the truth.

Blameworthy reflection is of two kinds:

The first: reflection on a false path, even if it is intended to reach the truth, for a false path does not lead to the truth.

The second: reflection and thinking that aims to refute the opponent's statement absolutely, whether it is true or false. He reflects in order to reject the statement of one he hates and opposes, by whatever means.

As for debate, it is divided into praiseworthy and blameworthy.

The praiseworthy is of two kinds, and the blameworthy is of two kinds.

The explanation of this is that the debater is either one who knows the truth, or one who seeks it,

or one who neither knows it nor seeks it.

This third is the blameworthy one.

As for the first two: whoever knows the truth, his praiseworthy debate is to make clear to another the proof that guides him if he is one seeking guidance and seeking the truth, or that cuts him off or breaks him if he is obstinate, not seeking the truth nor following it, or that halts him and prompts him to reflect on the proofs of the truth if he thinks he is upon the truth and his intention is the truth.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition, and argue with them in the best manner.﴾

So He mentioned the stages of da'wah (calling to Islam) and made them three categories according to the state of the one being called.

For he is either one who seeks the truth, desires it, loves it, and prefers it over other things once he knows it; this one is called with wisdom and needs neither admonition nor argument.

Or he is one who turns away and is occupied with the opposite of the truth, but if he came to know it, he would know it, prefer it and follow it; this one needs, along with wisdom, admonition through encouragement and warning.

Or he is one who is obstinate and opposing; this one is argued with in the best manner. If he returns to the truth, well and good; otherwise, one moves with him from argument to force (al-jilad), if possible.

So debating the one in falsehood has two benefits:

The first: that he is turned back from his falsehood and returns to the truth.

The second: that his evil and enmity are restrained, and it becomes clear to people that what he holds is falsehood. All these aspects cannot be attained by anything better than the proofs of the Qur'an and its debate with the sects, for it is sufficient for this in the most complete ways for whoever contemplates it, reflects upon it, and is granted understanding of it. Its proofs, although they are at the highest levels of proofs, are a method other than the method of the theologians (mutakallimun) and masters of dialectic and rational arguments. Rather, they are the closest thing to grasp, the clearest in indication, the strongest in demonstration, and the furthest from every doubt and suspicion.

[Section: The Second Degree: The Jealousy of the Seeker]

He said: The second degree is the jealousy of the seeker (al-murid). It is a jealousy over a time that has passed.

It is a deadly jealousy, for time is swift in its passing, proud of its side, slow in its return.

The "seekers" (al-muridun) are the people of spiritual states (ahl al-ahwal), and the "worshippers" (al-'ubbad) are the people of litanies and acts of worship (ahl al-awrad wa al-'ibadat). Every seeker is a worshipper, and every worshipper is a seeker. However, the people (al-qawm, i.e. the Sufis) have restricted the name "seeker" to the people of love and of the tasting of the realities of faith, and restricted the name "worshipper" to the people of mere action. Every seeker who is not a worshipper is a heretic (zindiq), and every worshipper who is not a seeker is a hypocrite (murai).

"Time" (al-waqt), for the worshipper, is the time of worship and litanies. For the seeker, it is the time of turning toward Allah, of being gathered upon Him, and of devoting oneself to Him with the whole heart.

"Time" is the most precious thing to him, and he is jealous over it lest it pass without that. When time has escaped him, he can never make it up at all, because the next time has already been allotted its own specific duty; so when a time is missed, there is no way for him to compensate for it.

As in the Musnad, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever breaks a fast on a day of Ramadan, deliberately and without an excuse, the fasting of a lifetime will not make it up for him, even if he fasts it."

His saying "and it is a deadly jealousy" means: harmful with a severe and clear harm resembling killing, for the anguish of loss is deadly, especially when the one who grieves knows that there is no way for him to make it up.

Also, jealousy over a loss is another loss, as it is said: occupation with regret over lost time is a waste of the present time. For this reason it is said: "Time is a sword: if you do not cut it, it will cut you."

Then the Shaykh explained the cause of why this jealousy is deadly. He said:

"For time is swift in its passing," i.e., quick to end, as the Arabs say "al-waha al-waha, al-ajal al-ajal" (hurry, hurry). Wahy means informing in secrecy and speed. It is said: "So-and-so came wahyan," i.e., came swiftly.

Time, then, passes by its very nature and departs of itself. Whoever neglects himself, his times pass away, his loss grows great, and his anguish intensifies. So how will his state be when, upon the realization of loss, he knows the measure of what he wasted, and seeks to return, but is barred from recovering it and from seeking to take hold of what has escaped him?

"How can yesterday be returned on a new day?" ﴿And how can they reach [the Faith] from a distant place?﴾ [Saba: 52], and he is prevented from what he loves and approves, and he knows that what he acquired is not what a sensible person should acquire, and he is barred from what he desires.

Poetry:
Oh, the anguish! There is no path to returning its like,
And if it were returned, the anguish would be easy.

These are the desires which had been,
They turned into anguish when patience became hard.

If they were returned with patience and strength,
They would turn into pleasures, and the one of intellect sees.

It is said: the most difficult of cut-off states is the cutting of breaths. For its people, when one breath rises, they send it up toward their Beloved, ascending to Him, clothed in love for Him and longing for Him. When they wish to push it away, they do not push it away until they follow it with another breath like it. So all their breaths are with Allah and toward Allah, clothed in His love, longing for Him, and intimacy with Him. None of their breaths with Allah escapes them except when sleep overcomes them. Many of them see in their sleep that they are in the same state, due to the mingling of their spirit and heart. So they keep watch over the times of their sleep and wakefulness. This state should not be denied, for when love overcomes the heart and takes possession of it, it necessarily brings this about for it.

The point is: passing experiences (al-waridat) are quickly gone; they pass faster than clouds, and time ends with what is in it. Nothing returns to you from it except its effect and its ruling. So choose for yourself what will return to you from your time, for it will certainly return to you. For this reason it is said to the happy: ﴿Eat and drink with ease for what you sent forward in the past days﴾ [al-Haqqah: 24], and it is said to the wretched: ﴿That is because you used to rejoice in the earth without right, and because you used to exult﴾ [Ghafir: 75].
